name: Trees, Graphs and Worst-Case Shapes
intent: See that the cost of a tree or graph algorithm depends on shape and representation, not just on n: a search tree is O(log n) only while it stays balanced, graph traversal is O(V + E) only with the right storage and a visited set, and the worst case often differs sharply from the typical one.
scenario: A service stores 1,000 user ids in a binary search tree. Tested with random ids, a lookup takes about 11 comparisons. In production the ids arrive in increasing order, the tree becomes a chain of height 1,000, and a lookup costs up to 1,000 comparisons. The same team stores a graph of 100,000 places as a V x V matrix and finds that it needs 10 billion cells.
problem: Big O statements about trees and graphs come with hidden conditions. 'Lookup in a search tree is O(log n)' assumes the tree is balanced, and a plain tree built from sorted keys is a linked list. 'Graph search is O(V + E)' assumes an adjacency list and a visited set; a matrix costs V squared whatever the number of edges, and a search that forgets what it has visited loops forever on any cycle. Tests on typical data hide all of this, and production data is often not typical.

howItWorks.title: A tree's cost is its height
howItWorks.text: Every operation on a binary search tree walks one path from the root, so it costs about the height. A balanced tree of n keys has height about log2 n (10 for 1,000 keys, 20 for a million). A plain tree built from random keys is usually close to that (height 21 for 1,000 random keys in the sample), but its shape follows the order of arrival: sorted or zig-zag keys give a chain of height 1,000, 499,500 comparisons to build and up to 1,000 per lookup.

howItWorks.title: Self-balancing trees guarantee the height
howItWorks.text: AVL and red-black trees rotate nodes after inserts and deletes so the height stays within a constant factor of log2 n whatever the order of the keys (an AVL tree's height is at most about 1.44 log2 n). On the sorted 1,000 keys an AVL tree has height 10 and needs 8,987 comparisons for 1,000 lookups instead of 500,500. A B-tree does the same with many keys per node, so the tree is only a few levels deep, which suits disks and database indexes. Ordered maps in standard libraries are typically balanced trees.

howItWorks.title: Graph search is O(V + E) with the right storage
howItWorks.text: Breadth-first and depth-first search take each vertex once and look at each edge once: V + 2E steps on an adjacency list, which stores only the edges that exist (V + 2E cells). An adjacency matrix has a cell for every pair of vertices, V squared in all: 10 billion cells for V = 100,000, and scanning a row to find neighbours makes the search cost V squared steps even when there are few edges. A matrix pays off only for small or dense graphs.

howItWorks.title: Remember where you have been
howItWorks.text: A graph with a cycle sends a search round it again and again unless visited vertices are marked, so a search without a visited set never ends. Recursive depth-first search also nests as deep as the longest path: a graph shaped like a path of 100,000 vertices needs 100,000 stack frames, which overflows the default stack in many runtimes (Python allows 1,000 by default). An explicit stack or a breadth-first search avoids that.

howItWorks.title: Choose the shortest-path algorithm for the graph
howItWorks.text: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from one source in a graph with non-negative weights. With a binary heap it takes about (V + 2E) log V steps in this model, which is O((V + E) log V); with a scan for the nearest vertex it takes about V squared: for V = 100,000 and 2 edges per vertex, roughly 8,500,000 steps against 10,000,400,000. And one search from the source finds the shortest path to every destination, so 100 separate searches for 100 destinations repeat the same work 100 times.

pros: Balanced trees and B-trees give ordered storage with guaranteed logarithmic operations
Adjacency lists make graph traversal proportional to the data that exists
A heap-based Dijkstra scales to large sparse graphs, such as road networks
Knowing the shape explains why the same code is fast in testing and slow in production
cons: Self-balancing trees are more complex and add a constant factor per insert
An adjacency list makes 'is there an edge between a and b' slower than a matrix lookup unless neighbours are kept in a set
Heaps and visited sets use extra memory, and a shortest-path search needs it for every vertex
Worst-case guarantees cost something on typical data that a simpler structure handles well
whenToUse: A balanced tree or B-tree when you need sorted order, range queries or predictable worst-case lookups
An adjacency list for large or sparse graphs, and a matrix only for small or dense ones
Dijkstra with a heap for weighted shortest paths with non-negative weights, and breadth-first search when every edge counts the same
whenNotToUse: A plain binary search tree for keys that can arrive sorted or nearly sorted
A V x V matrix for a large sparse graph
Recursive depth-first search on input whose depth is not bounded
Dijkstra with negative edge weights: it can give wrong answers, so use an algorithm built for them
pitfalls: Trusting the typical case: a plain binary search tree is fast on random keys and a chain on sorted keys, where lookups cost 1,000 comparisons instead of about 11 at n = 1,000

Reading O(log n) as small without asking what the tree looks like: the bound holds only for a balanced tree, and a deep chain can hide in it. The base matters too: a B-tree with a fan-out of 100 needs far fewer levels than a binary tree for the same keys
Recursive DFS on a long path: the recursion depth equals the path length, 100,000 frames for a path of 100,000 vertices, and overflows the default stack in many runtimes
Running a separate shortest-path search for every destination when one search from the source gives all of them: 100 searches cost 100 times as much
Forgetting the visited set: on any graph with a cycle the search loops forever and its queue keeps growing
Storing a large sparse graph as a matrix: V = 100,000 needs 10 billion cells, about 80 GB at 8 bytes a cell, even if there are only a few hundred thousand edges
Using Dijkstra's O(V squared) scan version on a large sparse graph: a binary heap makes it about (V + E) log V

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: Inserts keys, looks them up and asks for paths.

roles.label: Plain search tree
roles.description: Each insert descends from the root and attaches a leaf; no rebalancing.

roles.label: Balanced tree
roles.description: Rotates after inserts so the height stays near log2 n.

roles.label: Graph store
roles.description: An adjacency list (V + 2E cells) or a matrix (V x V cells).

roles.label: Graph search
roles.description: BFS, DFS or Dijkstra, with a visited set and a queue, stack or heap.

quiz.question: The keys 1, 2, 3, ... 1,000 are inserted in that order into a plain binary search tree with no balancing. What does the tree look like, and what does a lookup cost?
options: Height about 10, because a binary search tree is balanced by definition.
Height 1,000, a chain: a lookup can need up to 1,000 comparisons.
Height about 500, split evenly into a left and a right half.
Height 1,000, but lookups stay near 10 comparisons because keys are sorted.
quiz.explanation: Each new key is larger than all existing ones, so it becomes the right child of the last node: a linked list. Building costs 499,500 comparisons and lookups up to 1,000. A balanced (AVL or red-black) tree rotates to keep the height near 10.

quiz.question: A graph has 100,000 vertices and about 200,000 edges. How do an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list compare in memory?
options: Both need about 200,000 cells, because only edges are stored in either one.
The matrix needs about 500,000 cells and the list needs 10 billion.
The matrix needs 10 billion cells, the list about 500,000: it stores only existing edges.
The matrix needs about 100,000 cells, one for each vertex it records.
quiz.explanation: A matrix has a cell for every pair of vertices, V x V = 10 billion here, however few edges exist. A list needs V + 2E = 500,000 entries. For large sparse graphs, use a list; a matrix suits small or dense graphs.

quiz.question: A breadth-first search with no visited set runs on a graph that contains a cycle. What happens?
options: It never terminates: it keeps re-queuing vertices around the cycle, and the queue grows.
It finishes, only a constant factor slower, since it still goes level by level.
It finishes with exactly V + 2E steps, because breadth-first search never revisits a level.
It stops with an error the first time it meets a vertex it has already seen.
quiz.explanation: Without marking vertices as seen, every edge examined puts its endpoint in the queue again, so a cycle feeds itself forever (a capped run on a 100-vertex graph did not finish in 1,000,000 steps). The visited set is what makes the search O(V + E).
